questions.question: What is polymorphism in Java and what are its two types?
questions.title: Polymorphism in Java — Compile-Time and Runtime
questions.direct_answer: **Polymorphism** means 'many forms' — the same method name behaves differently in different contexts. Java has two types: **compile-time polymorphism** (method overloading — resolved at compile time) and **runtime polymorphism** (method overriding — resolved at runtime via dynamic dispatch).

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of both types of polymorphism and what distinguishes them
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing overloading with overriding, or not knowing which one is compile-time vs runtime
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that runtime polymorphism is the more powerful and commonly used form — it's the foundation of OOP design patterns

sections.title: One Interface, Multiple Behaviors
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Compile-time** polymorphism: method overloading, same class, different signatures, resolved at compile time
- **Runtime** polymorphism: method overriding, subclass, same signature, resolved at runtime
- Runtime polymorphism is enabled by virtual method dispatch (JVM checks actual object type)
- `@Override` annotation marks overriding methods — catches signature mismatches at compile time
- Runtime polymorphism requires: inheritance + method override + parent reference to child object
- Constructors and static methods are NOT polymorphic

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Polymorphism means 'many forms' and Java has two types. Compile-time polymorphism is method overloading — same method name, different parameter lists in the same class, resolved by the compiler. Runtime polymorphism is method overriding — a subclass provides its own implementation of a parent's method, and the JVM decides at runtime which version to call based on the actual object type. Runtime polymorphism is the more powerful form. It's what lets you write `Animal a = new Dog()` and have `a.sound()` automatically call Dog's version.

What is virtual method dispatch in Java?

questions.question: How does runtime polymorphism work with a parent reference pointing to a child object?
questions.title: Runtime Polymorphism — Parent Reference to Child Object
questions.direct_answer: When a parent reference holds a child object (`Animal a = new Dog()`), the reference type (`Animal`) determines what methods you can *call*, but the actual object type (`Dog`) determines *which implementation runs* at runtime. This is called **virtual method dispatch** or dynamic binding.

interviewer_intent.testing: Deep understanding of how the JVM resolves method calls at runtime vs compile time
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking the reference type determines which method runs — it only determines which methods are visible; the object type determines execution
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the practical benefit: you can write code against the Animal type and it works correctly for all subclasses without modification — the Open/Closed Principle

sections.title: Reference Type vs Object Type
Key Points
sections.content:
- Reference type: determines compile-time visibility of methods
- Object type: determines which implementation actually runs at runtime
- This is **virtual method dispatch** — JVM looks at the vtable of the actual object
- You cannot call subclass-specific methods through a parent reference without casting
- To call `fetch()`, you'd need: `((Dog) a).fetch()` with an `instanceof` check first
- Enables programming to interfaces/abstractions: code handles any subtype correctly
- Only works for **instance methods** — static methods use the reference type

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: When you have `Animal a = new Dog()`, two different things are happening at compile time and runtime. At compile time, the compiler uses the reference type — Animal — to check which methods you're allowed to call. If Animal doesn't have a `fetch()` method, you can't call it through that reference. But at runtime, when you call `a.sound()`, the JVM checks the actual object — which is a Dog — and calls Dog's version of `sound()`. This is virtual method dispatch. The benefit is that you can write code that works against the Animal type and it automatically works correctly for every subclass.

questions.question: What is method overloading in Java and what are the rules for it?
questions.title: Method Overloading Rules in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Method overloading** is defining multiple methods in the same class with the same name but different parameter lists. The compiler distinguishes them by the **number, type, or order of parameters**. Return type alone cannot distinguish overloaded methods.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowing the rules for overloading and the common gotcha about return type
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking you can overload by changing only the return type — this causes a compile error
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that overloading is resolved at compile time (static dispatch) and that auto-widening can cause surprising method selection

sections.title: Overloading — Same Name, Different Signature
Key Points
sections.content:
- Overloading requires different parameter lists (number, type, or order of params)
- Return type alone cannot distinguish overloaded methods — compile error
- Resolved at **compile time** based on argument types — static polymorphism
- Java applies widening promotion if no exact match (int → long → float → double)
- Auto-boxing: `print(5)` can match `print(Integer)` if no `print(int)` exists
- `null` can be ambiguous if multiple overloads accept reference types — explicit cast needed
- Overloading works across inheritance too — subclass can add overloads to parent's method

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Method overloading means having multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists in the same class. The compiler picks the right one at compile time based on the argument types. The key rule is that you must change the parameters — changing only the return type doesn't work and causes a compile error. One subtle thing to know is that Java applies widening promotion when there's no exact match, so calling with an `int` can match a `long` parameter if no `int` version exists — which can sometimes lead to unexpected method calls.

questions.question: What are the rules for method overriding in Java?
questions.title: Method Overriding Rules in Java
questions.direct_answer: For valid method overriding: the method must have the **same name and parameter list** as the parent method, the return type must be the same or a **covariant** (subtype), the access modifier must be the same or **more permissive**, and the method cannot throw broader checked exceptions. Use `@Override` to let the compiler verify.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of all the overriding rules, particularly covariant return types, access modifier widening, and exception rules
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing about covariant return types, or thinking you can narrow the access modifier (e.g., parent public → child private)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention @Override's role in catching typos and the covariant return type feature added in Java 5

sections.title: The Rules of Valid Overriding
Key Points
sections.content:
- Same method signature (name + params) is mandatory
- Covariant return types allowed since Java 5: child can return a subtype of parent's return type
- Access modifier can only be widened: `protected` → `public` is OK, reverse is not
- Checked exceptions: can throw same, fewer, or narrower — never broader checked exceptions
- `@Override` annotation: not required but strongly recommended — catches typos and invalid overrides
- Cannot override `final` methods (compile error)
- Cannot override `static` methods — that's method hiding, not overriding
- Cannot override `private` methods — they're not visible to the subclass

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: For a valid method override, the method must have the same name and parameter list as the parent's method. The return type must be the same or a subtype — this is called covariant return type. The access modifier can only be widened, not narrowed, so you can go from protected to public but not the other way. For checked exceptions, you can declare fewer or narrower ones but not broader ones. Also, you can't override final, static, or private methods. I always use @Override because it tells the compiler to verify that it's a valid override, catching typos early.

questions.question: What is the instanceof operator and when should you use it?
questions.title: instanceof Operator in Java
questions.direct_answer: `instanceof` checks whether an object is an instance of a specific class or implements an interface. It returns `true` if the object is of that type (or a subtype). It is used before **downcasting** to avoid `ClassCastException`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of instanceof and its role in safe downcasting
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using instanceof excessively — it can indicate poor polymorphism design if you're checking types to decide behavior
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Java 16+ pattern matching for instanceof: `if (a instanceof Dog d)` which combines check and cast

sections.title: instanceof for Safe Downcasting
Key Points
sections.content:
- Returns `true` if the object is an instance of the given type or any subtype
- `null instanceof T` always returns `false` — null-safe
- Use before downcasting to prevent `ClassCastException`
- Java 16+ pattern matching: `if (obj instanceof Dog d)` combines check and cast
- Excessive instanceof checks = design smell (should use polymorphism instead)
- Works with interfaces: `animal instanceof Runnable` checks if animal implements Runnable
- The `getClass()` method provides exact type check (no subtype matching)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The `instanceof` operator checks whether an object is of a specific type or a subtype, returning true or false. It's primarily used before downcasting to prevent ClassCastException — you check `if (a instanceof Dog)` before doing `(Dog) a`. Null is always false with instanceof, so it's null-safe. In Java 16+, pattern matching simplifies this to `if (a instanceof Dog d)` which combines the check and cast in one step. One thing worth mentioning: if you're using instanceof frequently to make decisions about behavior, that often means you should redesign to use polymorphism instead.

questions.question: What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding in Java?
questions.title: Method Overloading vs Overriding in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Overloading** is same method name with different parameters *in the same class*, resolved at **compile time**. **Overriding** is same method signature in a *subclass*, resolved at **runtime**. Overloading is about convenience; overriding is about polymorphism.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to clearly articulate the differences — this is one of the most commonly asked OOP comparison questions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Getting the compile-time vs runtime distinction backwards, or saying overloading is a form of inheritance
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use a comparison table format and give a practical code example for each

sections.title: Overloading vs Overriding — Side by Side
Overloading vs Overriding Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | Overloading | Overriding |
|---|---|---|
| Location | Same class | Subclass |
| Parameters | Must differ | Must be identical |
| Return type | Can differ | Same or covariant |
| Binding | Compile time (static) | Runtime (dynamic) |
| Inheritance | Not required | Required |
| @Override | Not applicable | Strongly recommended |
| Access modifier | Can differ freely | Can only be widened |
| Polymorphism type | Compile-time | Runtime |

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Overloading is in the same class — same method name, different parameter lists, resolved by the compiler at compile time. Overriding is in a subclass — same method name and same parameters as the parent, resolved by the JVM at runtime. So overloading is static binding and overriding is dynamic binding. Overloading is about making code convenient — `add(int, int)` and `add(double, double)`. Overriding is about polymorphism — making a subclass behave differently from the parent when called through a parent reference.
